service/networking.name: Networking
service/networking.html:
We design, install and fix wired and wireless networks for landlords, managing agents, offices, shops and homeowners, working from our base at 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE.

A network is more than a router. It is the position of the hub, the switch that links everything, the cable to each desk, TV, camera and access point, and the Wi-Fi that fills the gaps. We plan those together, so the building ends up with one tidy, documented system instead of a pile of boosters and loose leads.

Most of our networking work falls into four kinds of job: new installs in offices, shops and refurbished houses; HMO and block networks where tenant Wi-Fi has to be kept apart from CCTV and door entry; fault finding on networks that are slow or keep dropping; and reconnecting cameras, door stations and other building systems after a broadband provider changes the router.

Switches, guest Wi-Fi and the comms cabinet

Offices and shops usually need a proper switch, wired desks and printers, and Wi-Fi from ceiling access points. Guest Wi-Fi goes on its own network so visitors never see the office PCs, tills or cameras. A small UPS keeps the router and switch up through short power blips, which stops card machines and phones dropping.

Finding the fault, not guessing

When a network is slow or keeps dropping, the cause is usually physical cabling, a switch loop, an address conflict, PoE overload or Wi-Fi interference. We test the line speed at the hub first, then each cable, port and access point in turn, so the fix is aimed at the real problem. Where the problem is the provider's line, you get the readings to show them.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. We fit them flush where walls allow, or in surface boxes and trunking where chasing a Greater Manchester wall or a listed finish is not sensible. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

At the central point the cables terminate on a patch panel in a cabinet, where short patch leads connect them to the switch. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. For shared buildings in Greater Manchester we put the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard so tenants cannot unplug building systems.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

Between buildings, between floors of larger blocks and on any run longer than copper allows, fibre is the answer. It does not carry power, so a camera or access point at the far end still needs a local supply or a PoE switch fed from that building. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

PoE budgets for cameras, access points and door stations

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. An undersized switch is a common cause of cameras that vanish after dark in Greater Manchester properties we are called to. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

CCTV and door entry on a Sky or BT hub

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. The old method is port forwarding, which opens the recorder to the internet and needs redoing with every new router. Cloud or P2P apps connect outwards from the recorder instead, so nothing is opened on the router and the app keeps working after most changes.

We reserve the device's address in the hub's DHCP settings so it does not move. Without one, a power cut or hub restart can give the recorder a new address and the app, or any forwarded port, stops finding it.

A new hub from Sky or BT arrives with a new network name, password and blank settings, so Wi-Fi cameras and door stations lose their connection. The result is an app that says offline, even though the recorder in the cupboard is still recording. We rejoin the devices, re-reserve addresses, move to cloud or P2P where we can and leave the settings on record for the next swap.

Shared houses and blocks in Greater Manchester

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. Clear separation avoids the familiar problem of the building's cameras riding on a tenant's line that is then cancelled.

Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

A booster or extender listens to the router and rebroadcasts it, which costs speed and adds delay, especially through two walls. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

Wired ceiling access points, powered by PoE from a switch, are the step up for offices, HMOs and larger Greater Manchester houses. They are managed together, so channels and power are set to stop neighbouring units fighting each other. If a two-node mesh will fix the problem, we say so; if the building needs cabled access points, we explain why.

Dead spots in Greater Manchester buildings and how we find them

Thick brick walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors soak up the signal, so rooms two walls away from the router struggle. Foil-faced insulation, metal stud partitions, mirrors and appliances add to the loss, especially in extensions. Outbuildings, garden rooms and garages rarely get a usable signal from a router inside the house.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. In Greater Manchester flats and terraces, dozens of neighbouring networks compete for the same channels. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.

How we test and label every run

Structured cabling standards allow a 90 m permanent link from patch panel to outlet, with up to 10 m of patch leads in total. In a long Greater Manchester terrace, a mill conversion or a block with the comms cupboard at one end, we measure the route first, because a run that goes over length can work on the day and then drop out under load.

Each run is tested end to end after termination and the result is recorded against the outlet number. Labels match at both ends, so the next engineer, or your IT person, can find any port without guessing. That record matters when a landlord, a tenant or a future contractor needs to trace a fault.

Booking, the visit and what you get

Tell us the address and the problem or plan; photos of the router position and the rooms help us scope it. Same-day and next-day visits are available, and price is on application once we know the building and the scope. Phone or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At handover you get the test results, a labelled plan of points and access points, and the network names and admin details stored with you, not with us. Work is left neat, with cable fixed, holes made good and old kit removed if you want it gone.

Frequently asked questions

Do you work on networks you did not install?

Yes. We test and document what is there first, then fix, extend or replace only what needs it.

Can you separate tenant Wi-Fi from building systems?

Yes. In HMOs and blocks we put CCTV, door entry and other building kit on their own network or VLAN and give tenants a separate network.

Can visitors use our Wi-Fi safely?

Yes, on a separate guest network that cannot reach office PCs, tills or cameras.

What if the problem is my broadband line?

We test the line at the hub first. If the fault is on the provider's side, we give you the readings to take to them.

Can you add data points without chasing walls?

Often, yes. We drop cable inside stud walls, use floor voids and loft space, or fit neat surface trunking where walls are solid.

Is Cat5e still good enough?

For gigabit links to desks, TVs, cameras and door stations, yes. We fit Cat6 for most new points because it gives more headroom for little extra cost, and Cat6a or fibre where 10 Gb/s or long runs are needed.

What is a PoE budget?

The total power a PoE switch can supply across its ports. We add up the maximum draw of every camera, access point and door station, including night-time infrared, and leave headroom.

Will my CCTV work with a Sky or BT hub?

Yes. The systems we fit work with your Sky or BT hub. We set a DHCP reservation and use the recorder's cloud or P2P app where it has one, so remote viewing is not tied to port forwarding.

Should tenant Wi-Fi share a network with the CCTV?

No. We put building systems on their own network or VLAN, give tenants a separate network, and lock the cabinet in a landlord space.

Is mesh better than a Wi-Fi booster?

Usually. A booster repeats the signal and roughly halves speed for devices behind it; a mesh system works as one network, and with wired backhaul it performs far better.

Why is there no Wi-Fi upstairs?

Concrete or joisted floors, chimney breasts, foil-backed insulation and the hub's position by the front door are the usual causes. We measure each room before recommending a fix.

How long can an Ethernet cable run be?

90 m of fixed cable from patch panel to outlet, plus patch leads, for a 100 m channel. Longer runs need fibre or a switch part way.

How much does it cost?

Price on application. We confirm the scope first, then send a written quote before any work starts.

service/structured-cabling.meta: Structured data cabling, data points, patch panels, PoE and fibre links across Greater Manchester and the North West. Tested and labelled. Same/Next-Day, price on application.
service/structured-cabling.h1: Data cabling: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a, fibre, data points and PoE
service/structured-cabling.name: Data cabling
service/structured-cabling.html:
We install structured data cabling for homes, offices, HMOs and blocks: Cat5e, Cat6 and Cat6a copper, fibre between buildings and floors, data points, patch panels, comms cabinets and Power over Ethernet runs for cameras, access points and door stations.

Structured cabling means every outlet has its own cable back to a patch panel, every run is tested and every port is labelled at both ends. That is what makes later changes quick: a desk moves, a camera is added or a tenant needs a wired point, and the change is a patch lead in the cabinet rather than a new cable through the walls.

We cover single extra points, whole-house cabling during a refurbishment, office fit-outs and the cabling behind CCTV, door entry and intercom systems. Every job is surveyed and quoted in writing first.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

For links to a garage, a workshop or another block, and for long risers where copper would run out of length, fibre makes sense. It does not carry power, so a camera or access point at the far end still needs a local supply or a PoE switch fed from that building. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Run lengths, testing and labelling

Structured cabling standards allow a 90 m permanent link from patch panel to outlet, with up to 10 m of patch leads in total. In a long Greater Manchester terrace, a mill conversion or a block with the comms cupboard at one end, we measure the route first, because a run that goes over length can work on the day and then drop out under load.

Every outlet is tested after it is terminated, and the result goes on the handover sheet with its number. Both ends carry matching labels, so the faceplate number in a Greater Manchester bedroom or office matches the port on the patch panel. It saves time later, when a fault has to be traced or a point moved.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. In plastered walls we go flush where we can, and use surface trunking in solid walls, rented flats or finished rooms where chasing is unwelcome. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. It gives the router, switch and recorder a tidy, ventilated home instead of a tangle behind the sofa. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

PoE budgets for cameras, access points and door stations

PoE lets one cable carry both data and power to a camera, an access point or a door station. PoE comes in classes: 802.3af at about 15 W a port, 802.3at at about 30 W and 802.3bt for higher-power kit, all within the switch's total budget.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

Shared houses and blocks in Greater Manchester

In an HMO or block, tenant broadband and building systems such as CCTV, door entry and fire alarm signalling should not share one open network. That usually means a separate VLAN or a second router for building systems, tenant Wi-Fi on its own network, and a locked cabinet. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

Works with your Sky or BT hub: what to know

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. We prefer cloud or P2P access: the device connects out, nothing is opened inbound, and it copes with router changes better.

We also set a DHCP reservation on the hub so the recorder or door station always gets the same local address. If that is not done, a restart can hand out a different address and remote viewing quietly stops.

When a provider swaps the hub, which happens on upgrades and moves between Sky and BT, the Wi-Fi name, password, reservations and port rules all change. Wi-Fi cameras and doorbells drop off, forwarded ports vanish and the app shows the recorder offline even though it is still recording locally. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. The best results come when the nodes are joined by Ethernet backhaul, a cable between each node and the router, rather than by wireless.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are set up as one system, with channel and power planning so they cover rooms without interfering. If a two-node mesh will fix the problem, we say so; if the building needs cabled access points, we explain why.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Most dead spots come from the building itself: solid walls, chimney breasts, concrete floors and steel. Foil-backed plasterboard and insulation, mirrors, metal studs and underfloor heating pipes all cut signal further. Outbuildings, garden rooms and garages rarely get a usable signal from a router inside the house.

Hubs are often left where the line comes in, low down by the front door, which is one of the worst places for coverage. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. We test each room first, so you only pay for the fix the building actually needs.

Small office and shop networks

For a small office we plan the router, a switch with spare ports, and wired points for desks, printers and card machines. Guest Wi-Fi goes on its own network so visitors never see the office PCs, tills or cameras. A small UPS keeps the router and switch up through short power blips, which stops card machines and phones dropping.

Survey, quote and handover

Send the address, what is not working or what you want added, and photos of the router, cabinet and problem rooms if you can. Same-day or next-day visits can usually be arranged; the cost is price on application, set out in writing before work starts. You can reach us on 07517 806082 by phone or WhatsApp, or at icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

You are left with a list of what was fitted, the test results, labels that match the plan, and the admin passwords handed to you. Cables are clipped or in trunking, holes are made good, and old boosters or loose leads we replace are taken away.

Frequently asked questions

Do you label and test every run?

Yes. Each run is tested end to end after termination and labelled at the outlet and the patch panel, with results recorded at handover.

Can you cable an occupied house or office?

Yes. We plan routes through lofts, floor voids and stud walls and use neat trunking where walls are solid, working room by room.

Is Cat5e still good enough?

For gigabit links to desks, TVs, cameras and door stations, yes. We fit Cat6 for most new points because it gives more headroom for little extra cost, and Cat6a or fibre where 10 Gb/s or long runs are needed.

How long can an Ethernet cable run be?

90 m of fixed cable from patch panel to outlet, plus patch leads, for a 100 m channel. Longer runs need fibre or a switch part way.

Can you add data points without chasing walls?

Often, yes. We drop cable inside stud walls, use floor voids and loft space, or fit neat surface trunking where walls are solid.

What is a PoE budget?

The total power a PoE switch can supply across its ports. We add up the maximum draw of every camera, access point and door station, including night-time infrared, and leave headroom.

Should tenant Wi-Fi share a network with the CCTV?

No. We put building systems on their own network or VLAN, give tenants a separate network, and lock the cabinet in a landlord space.

Will my CCTV work with a Sky or BT hub?

Yes. The systems we fit work with your Sky or BT hub. We set a DHCP reservation and use the recorder's cloud or P2P app where it has one, so remote viewing is not tied to port forwarding.

Is mesh better than a Wi-Fi booster?

Usually. A booster repeats the signal and roughly halves speed for devices behind it; a mesh system works as one network, and with wired backhaul it performs far better.

Why is there no Wi-Fi upstairs?

Concrete or joisted floors, chimney breasts, foil-backed insulation and the hub's position by the front door are the usual causes. We measure each room before recommending a fix.

Can visitors use our Wi-Fi safely?

Yes, on a separate guest network that cannot reach office PCs, tills or cameras.

How much does it cost?

Price on application. We confirm the scope first, then send a written quote before any work starts.

service/wifi.meta: Mesh Wi-Fi, access points and dead-spot fixes, plus CCTV and door entry that works with your Sky or BT hub. Greater Manchester and the North West. Same/Next-Day, price on application.
service/wifi.h1: Wi-Fi and mesh Wi-Fi: dead spots, boosters, extenders and access points
service/wifi.name: Wi-Fi and mesh Wi-Fi
service/wifi.html:
We fix Wi-Fi that does not reach upstairs, the back bedroom, the loft conversion or the garden office, and we install Wi-Fi for HMOs, offices and shops where every room needs a usable signal.

We measure before we recommend anything. A room-by-room check of signal and speed shows whether the answer is moving the hub, adding a mesh node with wired backhaul, fitting ceiling access points on PoE, or simply replacing a booster that is halving your speed.

We also connect the building systems that depend on Wi-Fi: CCTV recorders, Wi-Fi cameras, video door entry and doorbells. They work with your Sky or BT hub, and we set them up so a router swap does not leave the app saying offline.

Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. Mesh Wi-Fi spreads several nodes around the property under one network name, and devices move between them as you walk around. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. They are managed together, so channels and power are set to stop neighbouring units fighting each other. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Most dead spots come from the building itself: solid walls, chimney breasts, concrete floors and steel. Foil-backed plasterboard and insulation, mirrors, metal studs and underfloor heating pipes all cut signal further. Outbuildings, garden rooms and garages rarely get a usable signal from a router inside the house.

Router position matters as much as the walls: a hub in a cupboard, behind the TV or by the front door at floor level loses much of its range. In Greater Manchester flats and terraces, dozens of neighbouring networks compete for the same channels. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Works with your Sky or BT hub: what to know

CCTV and door entry we install works with your Sky or BT hub, and the important choice is how remote viewing is set up. The old method is port forwarding, which opens the recorder to the internet and needs redoing with every new router. Cloud or P2P apps connect outwards from the recorder instead, so nothing is opened on the router and the app keeps working after most changes.

We reserve the device's address in the hub's DHCP settings so it does not move. Without one, a power cut or hub restart can give the recorder a new address and the app, or any forwarded port, stops finding it.

When a provider swaps the hub, which happens on upgrades and moves between Sky and BT, the Wi-Fi name, password, reservations and port rules all change. Cameras on Wi-Fi disconnect, port rules are gone and the app reports the system offline, while the recorder still records on site. We rejoin the devices, re-reserve addresses, move to cloud or P2P where we can and leave the settings on record for the next swap.

Choosing the cable grade for Greater Manchester sites

For a plain gigabit link to a desk, a smart TV or a door station, Cat5e does the job. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

Between buildings, between floors of larger blocks and on any run longer than copper allows, fibre is the answer. Fibre carries no power, which means the far end needs a media converter or switch with its own supply. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

PoE lets one cable carry both data and power to a camera, an access point or a door station. The switch has a total power budget in watts, and each port has a limit set by its standard: 802.3af gives up to about 15 W, 802.3at about 30 W and 802.3bt more again.

We total the maximum figures from the datasheets, not the typical ones, because night-time infrared and heaters push draw up. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. On longer runs we also check cable grade and length, since voltage drop on thin or copper-clad cable can starve a device.

Shared houses and blocks in Greater Manchester

In an HMO or block, tenant broadband and building systems such as CCTV, door entry and fire alarm signalling should not share one open network. That usually means a separate VLAN or a second router for building systems, tenant Wi-Fi on its own network, and a locked cabinet. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

Adding data points and a patch panel in Greater Manchester

Each data point is an outlet on the wall, usually single or double, with its own run back to the patch panel. We fit them flush where walls allow, or in surface boxes and trunking where chasing a Greater Manchester wall or a listed finish is not sensible. Common spots are the TV wall, home-office desks, the router position, ceiling access points and camera points.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

How we troubleshoot a slow or dropping network

When a network is slow or keeps dropping, the cause is usually physical cabling, a switch loop, an address conflict, PoE overload or Wi-Fi interference. We start at the incoming line, then test cables, switch ports and Wi-Fi in order, ruling things out one by one. Where the problem is the provider's line, you get the readings to show them.

Survey, quote and handover

Send the address, what is not working or what you want added, and photos of the router, cabinet and problem rooms if you can. Same-day and next-day visits are available, and price is on application once we know the building and the scope. Call or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

You are left with a list of what was fitted, the test results, labels that match the plan, and the admin passwords handed to you. We tidy as we go: cables are fixed, holes filled and replaced kit removed.

keyword/network-installation.html:
A new network for a Greater Manchester property means the right router position, a switch, cabled points where they matter and Wi-Fi that reaches every room.

We plan around how the building is used, then cable, configure and test it so it works from day one.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

Switches, guest Wi-Fi and the comms cabinet

Offices and shops usually need a proper switch, wired desks and printers, and Wi-Fi from ceiling access points. Guest Wi-Fi goes on its own network so visitors never see the office PCs, tills or cameras. A small UPS keeps the router and switch up through short power blips, which stops card machines and phones dropping.

Faceplates, back boxes and the comms cabinet

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. Flush back boxes are used where we can chase or drop cable inside a stud wall; elsewhere we use neat surface trunking. Typical positions are behind a TV, at a desk, by the router, at each access point and at camera or door-station locations.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. In Greater Manchester blocks and HMOs the cabinet usually sits in a locked landlord cupboard, apart from tenant areas.

Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre in Greater Manchester

Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Where access points, a server or a busy switch stack need 10 Gb/s along the whole run, Cat6a is the grade to specify, though it needs bigger containment.

For links to a garage, a workshop or another block, and for long risers where copper would run out of length, fibre makes sense. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Finding the fault, not guessing

Slow or dropping networks usually come down to a short list of causes: a failing cable or termination, a loop between switch ports, a duplicate address, an overloaded PoE switch, or Wi-Fi channel clashes. The method is simple: test the line, then the cabling, then the switch and then the Wi-Fi, recording each result. If it turns out to be the line, we give you the evidence to send to your provider.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. The switch has a total power budget in watts, and each port has a limit set by its standard: 802.3af gives up to about 15 W, 802.3at about 30 W and 802.3bt more again.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

CCTV and door entry on a Sky or BT hub

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding points a router port at the recorder; it works, but it puts the device on the internet and fails if the router is replaced. Cloud or P2P apps connect outwards from the recorder instead, so nothing is opened on the router and the app keeps working after most changes.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. Without a reservation, the address can change after a reboot and remote viewing drops.

Router swaps reset everything: Wi-Fi details, address reservations and any port forwarding. Wi-Fi cameras and doorbells drop off, forwarded ports vanish and the app shows the recorder offline even though it is still recording locally. We reconnect each device, set reservations on the new hub, move remote viewing to cloud or P2P where the recorder supports it, and write the settings down for next time.

Landlords and HMOs: tenant broadband and building systems

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. That usually means a separate VLAN or a second router for building systems, tenant Wi-Fi on its own network, and a locked cabinet. Clear separation avoids the familiar problem of the building's cameras riding on a tenant's line that is then cancelled.

Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

A plug-in extender or booster repeats the router's signal, and it usually halves the speed for devices connected through it because it receives and sends on the same radio. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

Dead spots in Greater Manchester buildings and how we find them

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-backed plasterboard and insulation, mirrors, metal studs and underfloor heating pipes all cut signal further. Outbuildings, garden rooms and garages rarely get a usable signal from a router inside the house.

Hubs are often left where the line comes in, low down by the front door, which is one of the worst places for coverage. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

The 90 m rule, test results and labels

Copper data cable has a 90 m limit for the fixed part of the run and 100 m including patch leads. Long routes are measured before we start, since an over-length run often works at first and then gives slow or dropping links.

Each run is tested end to end after termination and the result is recorded against the outlet number. Both ends carry matching labels, so the faceplate number in a Greater Manchester bedroom or office matches the port on the patch panel. Good records are what make later moves and fault finding quick and cheap.

Survey, quote and handover

Send the address, what is not working or what you want added, and photos of the router, cabinet and problem rooms if you can. Same-day or next-day visits can usually be arranged; the cost is price on application, set out in writing before work starts. Phone or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At handover you get the test results, a labelled plan of points and access points, and the network names and admin details stored with you, not with us. Cables are clipped or in trunking, holes are made good, and old boosters or loose leads we replace are taken away.

A small office in Greater Manchester needs reliable wired desks, Wi-Fi that covers meeting rooms and guest access kept separate.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

Small office and shop networks

Offices and shops usually need a proper switch, wired desks and printers, and Wi-Fi from ceiling access points. Guest and staff Wi-Fi are split so customers cannot reach office devices. A small UPS on the cabinet rides through power blips that otherwise reboot the router and drop calls.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. Flush back boxes are used where we can chase or drop cable inside a stud wall; elsewhere we use neat surface trunking. Typical positions are behind a TV, at a desk, by the router, at each access point and at camera or door-station locations.

At the central point the cables terminate on a patch panel in a cabinet, where short patch leads connect them to the switch. It gives the router, switch and recorder a tidy, ventilated home instead of a tangle behind the sofa. For shared buildings in Greater Manchester we put the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard so tenants cannot unplug building systems.

PoE budgets for cameras, access points and door stations

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. The switch has a total power budget in watts, and each port has a limit set by its standard: 802.3af gives up to about 15 W, 802.3at about 30 W and 802.3bt more again.

We total the maximum figures from the datasheets, not the typical ones, because night-time infrared and heaters push draw up. A switch that runs out of budget switches ports off, which looks like cameras dropping at night or a door station rebooting. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

Finding the fault, not guessing

Most network faults trace back to a damaged cable, a bad termination, a switch loop, an address clash, an overloaded PoE budget or crowded Wi-Fi channels. The method is simple: test the line, then the cabling, then the switch and then the Wi-Fi, recording each result. If it turns out to be the line, we give you the evidence to send to your provider.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6 gives more margin against interference and supports 10 Gb/s over short runs, so most Greater Manchester installs we do now use it. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Fibre carries no power, which means the far end needs a media converter or switch with its own supply. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

CCTV and door entry on a Sky or BT hub

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. The old method is port forwarding, which opens the recorder to the internet and needs redoing with every new router. Cloud or P2P connection has the recorder dial out to the maker's service, so no ports are opened and the app survives most router changes.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. Without one, a power cut or hub restart can give the recorder a new address and the app, or any forwarded port, stops finding it.

Router swaps reset everything: Wi-Fi details, address reservations and any port forwarding. The result is an app that says offline, even though the recorder in the cupboard is still recording. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Keeping tenant Wi-Fi apart from building systems

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. It keeps ownership clear when tenants change or a line is cancelled, which is a common cause of cameras going offline in Greater Manchester HMOs.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

A plug-in extender or booster repeats the router's signal, and it usually halves the speed for devices connected through it because it receives and sends on the same radio. Mesh systems use several nodes that work as one network with one name, and better ones keep a dedicated radio for the link between nodes. The best results come when the nodes are joined by Ethernet backhaul, a cable between each node and the router, rather than by wireless.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are managed together, so channels and power are set to stop neighbouring units fighting each other. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

Thick brick walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors soak up the signal, so rooms two walls away from the router struggle. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Hubs are often left where the line comes in, low down by the front door, which is one of the worst places for coverage. Neighbouring networks on the same channel, common in Greater Manchester terraces and flats, also slow things down. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.

Run lengths, testing and labelling

Copper data cable has a 90 m limit for the fixed part of the run and 100 m including patch leads. We measure the real route in Greater Manchester buildings, round corners and up risers, because runs that go over length tend to fail intermittently.

We test each link once it is terminated and record the pass against its label. Matching labels at the faceplate and the patch panel mean anyone can trace a port in seconds. It saves time later, when a fault has to be traced or a point moved.

Start by sending the address, a short description and, if possible, photos of the hub, any cabinet and the rooms affected. Same-day or next-day visits can usually be arranged; the cost is price on application, set out in writing before work starts. Call or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

You are left with a list of what was fitted, the test results, labels that match the plan, and the admin passwords handed to you. Work is left neat, with cable fixed, holes made good and old kit removed if you want it gone.

We repair broken network cabling and equipment in Greater Manchester properties, including cables cut during building work.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

Finding the fault, not guessing

Slow or dropping networks usually come down to a short list of causes: a failing cable or termination, a loop between switch ports, a duplicate address, an overloaded PoE switch, or Wi-Fi channel clashes. We test the line speed at the hub first, then each cable, port and access point in turn, so the fix is aimed at the real problem. If it turns out to be the line, we give you the evidence to send to your provider.

The 90 m rule, test results and labels

A copper Ethernet run is limited to 90 m of fixed cable, the permanent link, plus patch leads at each end, giving a 100 m channel. In a long Greater Manchester terrace, a mill conversion or a block with the comms cupboard at one end, we measure the route first, because a run that goes over length can work on the day and then drop out under load.

Each run is tested end to end after termination and the result is recorded against the outlet number. Labels match at both ends, so the next engineer, or your IT person, can find any port without guessing. That record matters when a landlord, a tenant or a future contractor needs to trace a fault.

Faceplates, back boxes and the comms cabinet

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. Flush back boxes are used where we can chase or drop cable inside a stud wall; elsewhere we use neat surface trunking. Typical positions are behind a TV, at a desk, by the router, at each access point and at camera or door-station locations.

All runs end at a patch panel, usually in a small wall cabinet with the switch and router alongside. Equipment then lives in one place with power and airflow, which helps reliability. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

Switches, guest Wi-Fi and the comms cabinet

A small office needs a router, a managed switch sized for the ports in use, and wired points for desks, printers and phones. Visitors get a separate guest network, isolated from the office machines and the till. A small UPS on the cabinet rides through power blips that otherwise reboot the router and drop calls.

Choosing the cable grade for Greater Manchester sites

Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

Between buildings, between floors of larger blocks and on any run longer than copper allows, fibre is the answer. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

PoE lets one cable carry both data and power to a camera, an access point or a door station. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

We total the maximum figures from the datasheets, not the typical ones, because night-time infrared and heaters push draw up. An undersized switch is a common cause of cameras that vanish after dark in Greater Manchester properties we are called to. Cheap copper-clad aluminium cable and long runs cause voltage drop, so we use solid copper for PoE.

Works with your Sky or BT hub: what to know

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding points a router port at the recorder; it works, but it puts the device on the internet and fails if the router is replaced. Cloud or P2P apps connect outwards from the recorder instead, so nothing is opened on the router and the app keeps working after most changes.

We also set a DHCP reservation on the hub so the recorder or door station always gets the same local address. Without a reservation, the address can change after a reboot and remote viewing drops.

Router swaps reset everything: Wi-Fi details, address reservations and any port forwarding. Cameras on Wi-Fi disconnect, port rules are gone and the app reports the system offline, while the recorder still records on site. We reconnect each device, set reservations on the new hub, move remote viewing to cloud or P2P where the recorder supports it, and write the settings down for next time.

Landlords and HMOs: tenant broadband and building systems

In shared houses and blocks we keep tenant internet separate from the landlord's CCTV, door entry and other building systems. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

A booster or extender listens to the router and rebroadcasts it, which costs speed and adds delay, especially through two walls. Mesh systems use several nodes that work as one network with one name, and better ones keep a dedicated radio for the link between nodes. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. We will say plainly when a simple mesh pair is enough and when cabling access points is worth it.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-faced insulation, metal stud partitions, mirrors and appliances add to the loss, especially in extensions. Outbuildings, garden rooms and garages rarely get a usable signal from a router inside the house.

Hubs are often left where the line comes in, low down by the front door, which is one of the worst places for coverage. Neighbouring networks on the same channel, common in Greater Manchester terraces and flats, also slow things down. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.

Tell us the address and the problem or plan; photos of the router position and the rooms help us scope it. Same-day or next-day visits can usually be arranged; the cost is price on application, set out in writing before work starts. Keeping tenant Wi-Fi apart from building systems

In an HMO or block, tenant broadband and building systems such as CCTV, door entry and fire alarm signalling should not share one open network. That usually means a separate VLAN or a second router for building systems, tenant Wi-Fi on its own network, and a locked cabinet. It keeps ownership clear when tenants change or a line is cancelled, which is a common cause of cameras going offline in Greater Manchester HMOs.

Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. Mesh Wi-Fi spreads several nodes around the property under one network name, and devices move between them as you walk around. Mesh works best with wired backhaul: each node gets a cable to the router, so its radios serve devices instead of relaying.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are set up as one system, with channel and power planning so they cover rooms without interfering. We will say plainly when a simple mesh pair is enough and when cabling access points is worth it.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. PoE comes in classes: 802.3af at about 15 W a port, 802.3at at about 30 W and 802.3bt for higher-power kit, all within the switch's total budget.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. Cheap copper-clad aluminium cable and long runs cause voltage drop, so we use solid copper for PoE.

Small office and shop networks

Offices and shops usually need a proper switch, wired desks and printers, and Wi-Fi from ceiling access points. Guest Wi-Fi goes on its own network so visitors never see the office PCs, tills or cameras. We often add a small UPS so brief power dips do not take the network down.

Most network faults trace back to a damaged cable, a bad termination, a switch loop, an address clash, an overloaded PoE budget or crowded Wi-Fi channels. Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

A plug-in extender or booster repeats the router's signal, and it usually halves the speed for devices connected through it because it receives and sends on the same radio. Mesh systems use several nodes that work as one network with one name, and better ones keep a dedicated radio for the link between nodes. Mesh works best with wired backhaul: each node gets a cable to the router, so its radios serve devices instead of relaying.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. They are managed together, so channels and power are set to stop neighbouring units fighting each other. We will say plainly when a simple mesh pair is enough and when cabling access points is worth it.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Most dead spots come from the building itself: solid walls, chimney breasts, concrete floors and steel. Foil-backed plasterboard and insulation, mirrors, metal studs and underfloor heating pipes all cut signal further. Outbuildings, garden rooms and garages rarely get a usable signal from a router inside the house.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. Neighbouring networks on the same channel, common in Greater Manchester terraces and flats, also slow things down. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.

Adding data points and a patch panel in Greater Manchester

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. In plastered walls we go flush where we can, and use surface trunking in solid walls, rented flats or finished rooms where chasing is unwelcome. At the central point the cables terminate on a patch panel in a cabinet, where short patch leads connect them to the switch. Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

For links to a garage, a workshop or another block, and for long risers where copper would run out of length, fibre makes sense. Power over Ethernet sends power down the data cable, so cameras, ceiling access points and many video door stations need no socket nearby. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre in Greater Manchester

Each data point is an outlet on the wall, usually single or double, with its own run back to the patch panel. We install structured cabling in Greater Manchester offices, blocks and HMOs, with every outlet numbered back to the patch panel.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

Faceplates, back boxes and the comms cabinet

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. We fit them flush where walls allow, or in surface boxes and trunking where chasing a Greater Manchester wall or a listed finish is not sensible. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

At the central point the cables terminate on a patch panel in a cabinet, where short patch leads connect them to the switch. Equipment then lives in one place with power and airflow, which helps reliability. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

How we test and label every run

A copper Ethernet run is limited to 90 m of fixed cable, the permanent link, plus patch leads at each end, giving a 100 m channel. We measure the real route in Greater Manchester buildings, round corners and up risers, because runs that go over length tend to fail intermittently.

We test each link once it is terminated and record the pass against its label. Labels match at both ends, so the next engineer, or your IT person, can find any port without guessing. Good records are what make later moves and fault finding quick and cheap.

Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre in Greater Manchester

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

We total the maximum figures from the datasheets, not the typical ones, because night-time infrared and heaters push draw up. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

Shared houses and blocks in Greater Manchester

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. The usual set-up is one network for building equipment, one for tenants, and the switch locked away in a landlord space. It keeps ownership clear when tenants change or a line is cancelled, which is a common cause of cameras going offline in Greater Manchester HMOs.

Works with your Sky or BT hub: what to know

CCTV and door entry we install works with your Sky or BT hub, and the important choice is how remote viewing is set up. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. Cloud or P2P connection has the recorder dial out to the maker's service, so no ports are opened and the app survives most router changes.

We also set a DHCP reservation on the hub so the recorder or door station always gets the same local address. If that is not done, a restart can hand out a different address and remote viewing quietly stops.

A new hub from Sky or BT arrives with a new network name, password and blank settings, so Wi-Fi cameras and door stations lose their connection. Wi-Fi cameras and doorbells drop off, forwarded ports vanish and the app shows the recorder offline even though it is still recording locally. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. The best results come when the nodes are joined by Ethernet backhaul, a cable between each node and the router, rather than by wireless.

Wired ceiling access points, powered by PoE from a switch, are the step up for offices, HMOs and larger Greater Manchester houses. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. In Greater Manchester flats and terraces, dozens of neighbouring networks compete for the same channels. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Small office and shop networks

A small office needs a router, a managed switch sized for the ports in use, and wired points for desks, printers and phones. Guest and staff Wi-Fi are split so customers cannot reach office devices. We often add a small UPS so brief power dips do not take the network down.

Survey, quote and handover

Send the address, what is not working or what you want added, and photos of the router, cabinet and problem rooms if you can. We offer same-day and next-day slots, and the price is on application after the scope is agreed. You can reach us on 07517 806082 by phone or WhatsApp, or at icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At the end you get test results, a simple plan of each point and node, and all passwords. We tidy as we go: cables are fixed, holes filled and replaced kit removed.

Neighbouring networks on the same channel, common in Greater Manchester terraces and flats, also slow things down. We test each room first, so you only pay for the fix the building actually needs.

Offices and shops usually need a proper switch, wired desks and printers, and Wi-Fi from ceiling access points. Guest Wi-Fi goes on its own network so visitors never see the office PCs, tills or cameras. We often add a small UPS so brief power dips do not take the network down.

keyword/fibre-cabling.html:
We install fibre links in Greater Manchester where copper would run out of length or would need to cross between buildings.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

Choosing the cable grade for Greater Manchester sites

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Where access points, a server or a busy switch stack need 10 Gb/s along the whole run, Cat6a is the grade to specify, though it needs bigger containment.

For links to a garage, a workshop or another block, and for long risers where copper would run out of length, fibre makes sense. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

Run lengths, testing and labelling

A copper Ethernet run is limited to 90 m of fixed cable, the permanent link, plus patch leads at each end, giving a 100 m channel. In a long Greater Manchester terrace, a mill conversion or a block with the comms cupboard at one end, we measure the route first, because a run that goes over length can work on the day and then drop out under load.

We test each link once it is terminated and record the pass against its label. Matching labels at the faceplate and the patch panel mean anyone can trace a port in seconds. It saves time later, when a fault has to be traced or a point moved.

Dead spots in Greater Manchester buildings and how we find them

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Router position matters as much as the walls: a hub in a cupboard, behind the TV or by the front door at floor level loses much of its range. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.

Faceplates, back boxes and the comms cabinet

A data point is a faceplate with one or two RJ45 sockets, fed by its own cable back to a patch panel. Flush back boxes are used where we can chase or drop cable inside a stud wall; elsewhere we use neat surface trunking. Typical positions are behind a TV, at a desk, by the router, at each access point and at camera or door-station locations.

All runs end at a patch panel, usually in a small wall cabinet with the switch and router alongside. Equipment then lives in one place with power and airflow, which helps reliability. In Greater Manchester blocks and HMOs the cabinet usually sits in a locked landlord cupboard, apart from tenant areas.

Power over Ethernet: sizing the switch

Power over Ethernet sends power down the data cable, so cameras, ceiling access points and many video door stations need no socket nearby. PoE comes in classes: 802.3af at about 15 W a port, 802.3at at about 30 W and 802.3bt for higher-power kit, all within the switch's total budget.

The budget is worked out from each device's maximum draw, with infrared, heaters and motors included, plus headroom for later additions. An undersized switch is a common cause of cameras that vanish after dark in Greater Manchester properties we are called to. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

Landlords and HMOs: tenant broadband and building systems

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. It keeps ownership clear when tenants change or a line is cancelled, which is a common cause of cameras going offline in Greater Manchester HMOs.

Router swaps, port forwarding and cloud apps

CCTV and door entry we install works with your Sky or BT hub, and the important choice is how remote viewing is set up. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. Cloud or P2P apps connect outwards from the recorder instead, so nothing is opened on the router and the app keeps working after most changes.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. If that is not done, a restart can hand out a different address and remote viewing quietly stops.

Router swaps reset everything: Wi-Fi details, address reservations and any port forwarding. Wi-Fi cameras and doorbells drop off, forwarded ports vanish and the app shows the recorder offline even though it is still recording locally. We reconnect each device, set reservations on the new hub, move remote viewing to cloud or P2P where the recorder supports it, and write the settings down for next time.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

A plug-in extender or booster repeats the router's signal, and it usually halves the speed for devices connected through it because it receives and sends on the same radio. Mesh Wi-Fi spreads several nodes around the property under one network name, and devices move between them as you walk around. Mesh works best with wired backhaul: each node gets a cable to the router, so its radios serve devices instead of relaying.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. They are set up as one system, with channel and power planning so they cover rooms without interfering. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

Small office and shop networks

Offices and shops usually need a proper switch, wired desks and printers, and Wi-Fi from ceiling access points. Visitors get a separate guest network, isolated from the office machines and the till. A small UPS keeps the router and switch up through short power blips, which stops card machines and phones dropping.

Survey, quote and handover

Tell us the address and the problem or plan; photos of the router position and the rooms help us scope it. We offer same-day and next-day slots, and the price is on application after the scope is agreed. Call or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At handover you get the test results, a labelled plan of points and access points, and the network names and admin details stored with you, not with us. Work is left neat, with cable fixed, holes made good and old kit removed if you want it gone.

Adding data points and a patch panel in Greater Manchester

Each data point is an outlet on the wall, usually single or double, with its own run back to the patch panel. Flush back boxes are used where we can chase or drop cable inside a stud wall; elsewhere we use neat surface trunking. Common spots are the TV wall, home-office desks, the router position, ceiling access points and camera points.

All runs end at a patch panel, usually in a small wall cabinet with the switch and router alongside. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. In Greater Manchester blocks and HMOs the cabinet usually sits in a locked landlord cupboard, apart from tenant areas.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 gives more margin against interference and supports 10 Gb/s over short runs, so most Greater Manchester installs we do now use it. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

Between buildings, between floors of larger blocks and on any run longer than copper allows, fibre is the answer. It does not carry power, so a camera or access point at the far end still needs a local supply or a PoE switch fed from that building. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

How we test and label every run

Structured cabling standards allow a 90 m permanent link from patch panel to outlet, with up to 10 m of patch leads in total. We measure the real route in Greater Manchester buildings, round corners and up risers, because runs that go over length tend to fail intermittently.

We test each link once it is terminated and record the pass against its label. Labels match at both ends, so the next engineer, or your IT person, can find any port without guessing. Good records are what make later moves and fault finding quick and cheap.

PoE budgets for cameras, access points and door stations

Power over Ethernet sends power down the data cable, so cameras, ceiling access points and many video door stations need no socket nearby. The switch has a total power budget in watts, and each port has a limit set by its standard: 802.3af gives up to about 15 W, 802.3at about 30 W and 802.3bt more again.

We total the maximum figures from the datasheets, not the typical ones, because night-time infrared and heaters push draw up. An undersized switch is a common cause of cameras that vanish after dark in Greater Manchester properties we are called to. On longer runs we also check cable grade and length, since voltage drop on thin or copper-clad cable can starve a device.

In shared houses and blocks we keep tenant internet separate from the landlord's CCTV, door entry and other building systems. Router position matters as much as the walls: a hub in a cupboard, behind the TV or by the front door at floor level loses much of its range. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Additional data points in Greater Manchester: extending an existing network with extra wired sockets.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

Faceplates, back boxes and the comms cabinet

A data point is a faceplate with one or two RJ45 sockets, fed by its own cable back to a patch panel. In plastered walls we go flush where we can, and use surface trunking in solid walls, rented flats or finished rooms where chasing is unwelcome. Typical positions are behind a TV, at a desk, by the router, at each access point and at camera or door-station locations.

All runs end at a patch panel, usually in a small wall cabinet with the switch and router alongside. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. For shared buildings in Greater Manchester we put the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard so tenants cannot unplug building systems.

How we test and label every run

A copper Ethernet run is limited to 90 m of fixed cable, the permanent link, plus patch leads at each end, giving a 100 m channel. In a long Greater Manchester terrace, a mill conversion or a block with the comms cupboard at one end, we measure the route first, because a run that goes over length can work on the day and then drop out under load.

We test each link once it is terminated and record the pass against its label. Both ends carry matching labels, so the faceplate number in a Greater Manchester bedroom or office matches the port on the patch panel. It saves time later, when a fault has to be traced or a point moved.

Switches, guest Wi-Fi and the comms cabinet

For a small office we plan the router, a switch with spare ports, and wired points for desks, printers and card machines. Guest Wi-Fi goes on its own network so visitors never see the office PCs, tills or cameras. A small UPS on the cabinet rides through power blips that otherwise reboot the router and drop calls.

Choosing the cable grade for Greater Manchester sites

For a plain gigabit link to a desk, a smart TV or a door station, Cat5e does the job. Cat6 gives more margin against interference and supports 10 Gb/s over short runs, so most Greater Manchester installs we do now use it. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

PoE lets one cable carry both data and power to a camera, an access point or a door station. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

We total the maximum figures from the datasheets, not the typical ones, because night-time infrared and heaters push draw up. A switch that runs out of budget switches ports off, which looks like cameras dropping at night or a door station rebooting. Cheap copper-clad aluminium cable and long runs cause voltage drop, so we use solid copper for PoE.

Keeping tenant Wi-Fi apart from building systems

In shared houses and blocks we keep tenant internet separate from the landlord's CCTV, door entry and other building systems. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. It keeps ownership clear when tenants change or a line is cancelled, which is a common cause of cameras going offline in Greater Manchester HMOs.

Router swaps, port forwarding and cloud apps

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. We prefer cloud or P2P access: the device connects out, nothing is opened inbound, and it copes with router changes better.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. Without a reservation, the address can change after a reboot and remote viewing drops.

When a provider swaps the hub, which happens on upgrades and moves between Sky and BT, the Wi-Fi name, password, reservations and port rules all change. Cameras on Wi-Fi disconnect, port rules are gone and the app reports the system offline, while the recorder still records on site. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Mesh, extenders, boosters or wired access points

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. Mesh Wi-Fi spreads several nodes around the property under one network name, and devices move between them as you walk around. The best results come when the nodes are joined by Ethernet backhaul, a cable between each node and the router, rather than by wireless.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are set up as one system, with channel and power planning so they cover rooms without interfering. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

Thick brick walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors soak up the signal, so rooms two walls away from the router struggle. Foil-faced insulation, metal stud partitions, mirrors and appliances add to the loss, especially in extensions. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.
