job/fibre-termination.html:
When fibre has been run but not finished, we terminate and test it in Greater Manchester.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

What happens on the day

We prepare the fibre, fit connectors or splice to pigtails in a tray, mount the panel and test each fibre. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

Choosing the cable grade for Greater Manchester sites

For a plain gigabit link to a desk, a smart TV or a door station, Cat5e does the job. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Where access points, a server or a busy switch stack need 10 Gb/s along the whole run, Cat6a is the grade to specify, though it needs bigger containment.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

The 90 m rule, test results and labels

A copper Ethernet run is limited to 90 m of fixed cable, the permanent link, plus patch leads at each end, giving a 100 m channel. In a long Greater Manchester terrace, a mill conversion or a block with the comms cupboard at one end, we measure the route first, because a run that goes over length can work on the day and then drop out under load.

Each run is tested end to end after termination and the result is recorded against the outlet number. Both ends carry matching labels, so the faceplate number in a Greater Manchester bedroom or office matches the port on the patch panel. It saves time later, when a fault has to be traced or a point moved.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

A data point is a faceplate with one or two RJ45 sockets, fed by its own cable back to a patch panel. Flush back boxes are used where we can chase or drop cable inside a stud wall; elsewhere we use neat surface trunking. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. It gives the router, switch and recorder a tidy, ventilated home instead of a tangle behind the sofa. For shared buildings in Greater Manchester we put the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard so tenants cannot unplug building systems.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

PoE lets one cable carry both data and power to a camera, an access point or a door station. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

We total the maximum figures from the datasheets, not the typical ones, because night-time infrared and heaters push draw up. A switch that runs out of budget switches ports off, which looks like cameras dropping at night or a door station rebooting. Cheap copper-clad aluminium cable and long runs cause voltage drop, so we use solid copper for PoE.

Keeping tenant Wi-Fi apart from building systems

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

CCTV and door entry on a Sky or BT hub

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. We prefer cloud or P2P access: the device connects out, nothing is opened inbound, and it copes with router changes better.

We also set a DHCP reservation on the hub so the recorder or door station always gets the same local address. Without one, a power cut or hub restart can give the recorder a new address and the app, or any forwarded port, stops finding it.

When a provider swaps the hub, which happens on upgrades and moves between Sky and BT, the Wi-Fi name, password, reservations and port rules all change. Wi-Fi cameras and doorbells drop off, forwarded ports vanish and the app shows the recorder offline even though it is still recording locally. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. If a two-node mesh will fix the problem, we say so; if the building needs cabled access points, we explain why.

Why the signal dies upstairs or at the back

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-faced insulation, metal stud partitions, mirrors and appliances add to the loss, especially in extensions. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Small office and shop networks

For a small office we plan the router, a switch with spare ports, and wired points for desks, printers and card machines. Guest Wi-Fi goes on its own network so visitors never see the office PCs, tills or cameras. A small UPS on the cabinet rides through power blips that otherwise reboot the router and drop calls.

Send the address, what is not working or what you want added, and photos of the router, cabinet and problem rooms if you can. Same-day or next-day visits can usually be arranged; the cost is price on application, set out in writing before work starts. Phone or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At the end you get test results, a simple plan of each point and node, and all passwords. Cables are clipped or in trunking, holes are made good, and old boosters or loose leads we replace are taken away.

job/data-point-installation.html:
Need a wired socket behind the TV, at a desk or for a camera in Greater Manchester? We install data points and test them.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

What happens on the day

We agree each point position, run the cable, fit the faceplate, terminate the patch panel end and test it. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

Faceplates, back boxes and the comms cabinet

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. We fit them flush where walls allow, or in surface boxes and trunking where chasing a Greater Manchester wall or a listed finish is not sensible. Common spots are the TV wall, home-office desks, the router position, ceiling access points and camera points.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. Equipment then lives in one place with power and airflow, which helps reliability. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

For links to a garage, a workshop or another block, and for long risers where copper would run out of length, fibre makes sense. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. We will tell you which grade fits the job in Greater Manchester, and why, before any cable goes in.

The 90 m rule, test results and labels

A copper Ethernet run is limited to 90 m of fixed cable, the permanent link, plus patch leads at each end, giving a 100 m channel. Long routes are measured before we start, since an over-length run often works at first and then gives slow or dropping links.

Each run is tested end to end after termination and the result is recorded against the outlet number. Labels match at both ends, so the next engineer, or your IT person, can find any port without guessing. That record matters when a landlord, a tenant or a future contractor needs to trace a fault.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

Power over Ethernet sends power down the data cable, so cameras, ceiling access points and many video door stations need no socket nearby. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. An undersized switch is a common cause of cameras that vanish after dark in Greater Manchester properties we are called to. On longer runs we also check cable grade and length, since voltage drop on thin or copper-clad cable can starve a device.

Shared houses and blocks in Greater Manchester

In an HMO or block, tenant broadband and building systems such as CCTV, door entry and fire alarm signalling should not share one open network. That usually means a separate VLAN or a second router for building systems, tenant Wi-Fi on its own network, and a locked cabinet. Clear separation avoids the familiar problem of the building's cameras riding on a tenant's line that is then cancelled.

Router swaps, port forwarding and cloud apps

Every recorder, camera and video door station we fit works with your Sky or BT hub; the question is how the app reaches it from outside. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. Cloud or P2P connection has the recorder dial out to the maker's service, so no ports are opened and the app survives most router changes.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. Without a reservation, the address can change after a reboot and remote viewing drops.

Router swaps reset everything: Wi-Fi details, address reservations and any port forwarding. The result is an app that says offline, even though the recorder in the cupboard is still recording. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

A booster or extender listens to the router and rebroadcasts it, which costs speed and adds delay, especially through two walls. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are managed together, so channels and power are set to stop neighbouring units fighting each other. If a two-node mesh will fix the problem, we say so; if the building needs cabled access points, we explain why.

Dead spots in Greater Manchester buildings and how we find them

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-backed plasterboard and insulation, mirrors, metal studs and underfloor heating pipes all cut signal further. Outbuildings, garden rooms and garages rarely get a usable signal from a router inside the house.

Router position matters as much as the walls: a hub in a cupboard, behind the TV or by the front door at floor level loses much of its range. Neighbouring networks on the same channel, common in Greater Manchester terraces and flats, also slow things down. We test each room first, so you only pay for the fix the building actually needs.

Small office and shop networks

For a small office we plan the router, a switch with spare ports, and wired points for desks, printers and card machines. Guest and staff Wi-Fi are split so customers cannot reach office devices. A small UPS keeps the router and switch up through short power blips, which stops card machines and phones dropping.

Survey, quote and handover

Tell us the address and the problem or plan; photos of the router position and the rooms help us scope it. We offer same-day and next-day slots, and the price is on application after the scope is agreed. Phone or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At handover you get the test results, a labelled plan of points and access points, and the network names and admin details stored with you, not with us. We tidy as we go: cables are fixed, holes filled and replaced kit removed.

PoE installation in Greater Manchester: Power over Ethernet for cameras, ceiling access points and video door stations.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

What happens on the day

We calculate the PoE budget, run solid copper cable, fit the PoE switch and confirm each device powers up and links. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

Power over Ethernet: sizing the switch

Power over Ethernet sends power down the data cable, so cameras, ceiling access points and many video door stations need no socket nearby. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

The budget is worked out from each device's maximum draw, with infrared, heaters and motors included, plus headroom for later additions. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. It does not carry power, so a camera or access point at the far end still needs a local supply or a PoE switch fed from that building. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

Router swaps, port forwarding and cloud apps

CCTV and door entry we install works with your Sky or BT hub, and the important choice is how remote viewing is set up. The old method is port forwarding, which opens the recorder to the internet and needs redoing with every new router. We prefer cloud or P2P access: the device connects out, nothing is opened inbound, and it copes with router changes better.

We also set a DHCP reservation on the hub so the recorder or door station always gets the same local address. Without a reservation, the address can change after a reboot and remote viewing drops.

Router swaps reset everything: Wi-Fi details, address reservations and any port forwarding. The result is an app that says offline, even though the recorder in the cupboard is still recording. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

How we test and label every run

Copper data cable has a 90 m limit for the fixed part of the run and 100 m including patch leads. We measure the real route in Greater Manchester buildings, round corners and up risers, because runs that go over length tend to fail intermittently.

Each run is tested end to end after termination and the result is recorded against the outlet number. Matching labels at the faceplate and the patch panel mean anyone can trace a port in seconds. That record matters when a landlord, a tenant or a future contractor needs to trace a fault.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

A data point is a faceplate with one or two RJ45 sockets, fed by its own cable back to a patch panel. In plastered walls we go flush where we can, and use surface trunking in solid walls, rented flats or finished rooms where chasing is unwelcome. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. It gives the router, switch and recorder a tidy, ventilated home instead of a tangle behind the sofa. For shared buildings in Greater Manchester we put the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard so tenants cannot unplug building systems.

Landlords and HMOs: tenant broadband and building systems

In shared houses and blocks we keep tenant internet separate from the landlord's CCTV, door entry and other building systems. That usually means a separate VLAN or a second router for building systems, tenant Wi-Fi on its own network, and a locked cabinet. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. Mesh systems use several nodes that work as one network with one name, and better ones keep a dedicated radio for the link between nodes. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. If a two-node mesh will fix the problem, we say so; if the building needs cabled access points, we explain why.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-faced insulation, metal stud partitions, mirrors and appliances add to the loss, especially in extensions. An outbuilding or garden office normally needs its own cabled or point-to-point link, not a booster on the windowsill.

Hubs are often left where the line comes in, low down by the front door, which is one of the worst places for coverage. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Switches, guest Wi-Fi and the comms cabinet

A small office needs a router, a managed switch sized for the ports in use, and wired points for desks, printers and phones. Visitors get a separate guest network, isolated from the office machines and the till. A small UPS keeps the router and switch up through short power blips, which stops card machines and phones dropping.

Start by sending the address, a short description and, if possible, photos of the hub, any cabinet and the rooms affected. Same-day and next-day visits are available, and price is on application once we know the building and the scope. You can reach us on 07517 806082 by phone or WhatsApp, or at icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At handover you get the test results, a labelled plan of points and access points, and the network names and admin details stored with you, not with us. Cables are clipped or in trunking, holes are made good, and old boosters or loose leads we replace are taken away.

We fix Wi-Fi dead spots in Greater Manchester homes, offices and HMOs, from the back bedroom to the loft conversion.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

What happens on the day

We measure signal in each room, find the cause, then reposition the hub, add a wired node or access point and retest. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Thick brick walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors soak up the signal, so rooms two walls away from the router struggle. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. An outbuilding or garden office normally needs its own cabled or point-to-point link, not a booster on the windowsill.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Mesh, extenders, boosters or wired access points

A booster or extender listens to the router and rebroadcasts it, which costs speed and adds delay, especially through two walls. Mesh Wi-Fi spreads several nodes around the property under one network name, and devices move between them as you walk around. Mesh works best with wired backhaul: each node gets a cable to the router, so its radios serve devices instead of relaying.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

Each data point is an outlet on the wall, usually single or double, with its own run back to the patch panel. In plastered walls we go flush where we can, and use surface trunking in solid walls, rented flats or finished rooms where chasing is unwelcome. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

At the central point the cables terminate on a patch panel in a cabinet, where short patch leads connect them to the switch. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

Works with your Sky or BT hub: what to know

Every recorder, camera and video door station we fit works with your Sky or BT hub; the question is how the app reaches it from outside. Port forwarding points a router port at the recorder; it works, but it puts the device on the internet and fails if the router is replaced. Cloud or P2P connection has the recorder dial out to the maker's service, so no ports are opened and the app survives most router changes.

We reserve the device's address in the hub's DHCP settings so it does not move. If that is not done, a restart can hand out a different address and remote viewing quietly stops.

A new hub from Sky or BT arrives with a new network name, password and blank settings, so Wi-Fi cameras and door stations lose their connection. Cameras on Wi-Fi disconnect, port rules are gone and the app reports the system offline, while the recorder still records on site. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

PoE budgets for cameras, access points and door stations

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. PoE comes in classes: 802.3af at about 15 W a port, 802.3at at about 30 W and 802.3bt for higher-power kit, all within the switch's total budget.

The budget is worked out from each device's maximum draw, with infrared, heaters and motors included, plus headroom for later additions. A switch that runs out of budget switches ports off, which looks like cameras dropping at night or a door station rebooting. On longer runs we also check cable grade and length, since voltage drop on thin or copper-clad cable can starve a device.

Landlords and HMOs: tenant broadband and building systems

In shared houses and blocks we keep tenant internet separate from the landlord's CCTV, door entry and other building systems. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

Fault finding in Greater Manchester

When a network is slow or keeps dropping, the cause is usually physical cabling, a switch loop, an address conflict, PoE overload or Wi-Fi interference. We test the line speed at the hub first, then each cable, port and access point in turn, so the fix is aimed at the real problem. Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. The best results come when the nodes are joined by Ethernet backhaul, a cable between each node and the router, rather than by wireless.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are set up as one system, with channel and power planning so they cover rooms without interfering. We will say plainly when a simple mesh pair is enough and when cabling access points is worth it.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. Without one, a power cut or hub restart can give the recorder a new address and the app, or any forwarded port, stops finding it.

Between buildings, between floors of larger blocks and on any run longer than copper allows, fibre is the answer. An extender in the wrong spot does little; we place and connect it properly in Greater Manchester.

What happens on the day

We test the signal, fit the extender with a cable where possible, configure it and retest. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

A plug-in extender or booster repeats the router's signal, and it usually halves the speed for devices connected through it because it receives and sends on the same radio. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are managed together, so channels and power are set to stop neighbouring units fighting each other. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Router position matters as much as the walls: a hub in a cupboard, behind the TV or by the front door at floor level loses much of its range. Neighbouring networks on the same channel, common in Greater Manchester terraces and flats, also slow things down. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Adding data points and a patch panel in Greater Manchester

A wired data point is simply a socket on the wall with its own cable running back to a central patch panel. In plastered walls we go flush where we can, and use surface trunking in solid walls, rented flats or finished rooms where chasing is unwelcome. Common spots are the TV wall, home-office desks, the router position, ceiling access points and camera points.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

CCTV and door entry on a Sky or BT hub

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding points a router port at the recorder; it works, but it puts the device on the internet and fails if the router is replaced. Cloud or P2P apps connect outwards from the recorder instead, so nothing is opened on the router and the app keeps working after most changes.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. If that is not done, a restart can hand out a different address and remote viewing quietly stops.

A new hub from Sky or BT arrives with a new network name, password and blank settings, so Wi-Fi cameras and door stations lose their connection. The result is an app that says offline, even though the recorder in the cupboard is still recording. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

For a plain gigabit link to a desk, a smart TV or a door station, Cat5e does the job. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Cat6a is worth it for backbone runs and high-end access points; it is bulkier, so we check trunking and bend space before quoting it.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Fibre carries no power, which means the far end needs a media converter or switch with its own supply. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

PoE budgets for cameras, access points and door stations

PoE lets one cable carry both data and power to a camera, an access point or a door station. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

The budget is worked out from each device's maximum draw, with infrared, heaters and motors included, plus headroom for later additions. A switch that runs out of budget switches ports off, which looks like cameras dropping at night or a door station rebooting. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. We use a separate network or VLAN for building kit, a guest or tenant network for residents, and the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

Slow or dropping networks usually come down to a short list of causes: a failing cable or termination, a loop between switch ports, a duplicate address, an overloaded PoE switch, or Wi-Fi channel clashes. We test the line speed at the hub first, then each cable, port and access point in turn, so the fix is aimed at the real problem. If the fault is with the broadband line itself, we give you the test results to take to the provider.

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-faced insulation, metal stud partitions, mirrors and appliances add to the loss, especially in extensions. An outbuilding or garden office normally needs its own cabled or point-to-point link, not a booster on the windowsill.

Hubs are often left where the line comes in, low down by the front door, which is one of the worst places for coverage. Every recorder, camera and video door station we fit works with your Sky or BT hub; the question is how the app reaches it from outside. Finding the fault, not guessing

We start at the incoming line, then test cables, switch ports and Wi-Fi in order, ruling things out one by one. If it turns out to be the line, we give you the evidence to send to your provider.

What is the difference between an access point and a booster?

An access point is cabled to the network and broadcasts at full speed; a booster repeats a weak signal and loses speed.

Do access points need a socket?

Is mesh better than a Wi-Fi booster?

Usually. A booster repeats the signal and roughly halves speed for devices behind it; a mesh system works as one network, and with wired backhaul it performs far better.

What is a PoE budget?

The total power a PoE switch can supply across its ports. We add up the maximum draw of every camera, access point and door station, including night-time infrared, and leave headroom.

Is Cat5e still good enough?

For gigabit links to desks, TVs, cameras and door stations, yes. We fit Cat6 for most new points because it gives more headroom for little extra cost, and Cat6a or fibre where 10 Gb/s or long runs are needed.

Why is there no Wi-Fi upstairs?

Concrete or joisted floors, chimney breasts, foil-backed insulation and the hub's position by the front door are the usual causes. We measure each room before recommending a fix.

Will my CCTV work with a Sky or BT hub?

What happens on the day

We test each room, cable access points to a locked cabinet, set up tenant and building networks and retest every room. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

Keeping tenant Wi-Fi apart from building systems

In shared houses and blocks we keep tenant internet separate from the landlord's CCTV, door entry and other building systems. The usual set-up is one network for building equipment, one for tenants, and the switch locked away in a landlord space. Clear separation avoids the familiar problem of the building's cameras riding on a tenant's line that is then cancelled.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. Mesh systems use several nodes that work as one network with one name, and better ones keep a dedicated radio for the link between nodes. Wire the nodes together with Ethernet backhaul and a mesh system performs close to wired access points.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

Dead spots in Greater Manchester buildings and how we find them

Thick brick walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors soak up the signal, so rooms two walls away from the router struggle. Foil-backed plasterboard and insulation, mirrors, metal studs and underfloor heating pipes all cut signal further. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. In Greater Manchester flats and terraces, dozens of neighbouring networks compete for the same channels. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.

Router swaps, port forwarding and cloud apps

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding points a router port at the recorder; it works, but it puts the device on the internet and fails if the router is replaced. We prefer cloud or P2P access: the device connects out, nothing is opened inbound, and it copes with router changes better.

We reserve the device's address in the hub's DHCP settings so it does not move. If that is not done, a restart can hand out a different address and remote viewing quietly stops.

A new hub from Sky or BT arrives with a new network name, password and blank settings, so Wi-Fi cameras and door stations lose their connection. Cameras on Wi-Fi disconnect, port rules are gone and the app reports the system offline, while the recorder still records on site. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Which cable suits a Greater Manchester building: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre

Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Fibre carries no power, which means the far end needs a media converter or switch with its own supply. We will tell you which grade fits the job in Greater Manchester, and why, before any cable goes in.

PoE budgets for cameras, access points and door stations

PoE lets one cable carry both data and power to a camera, an access point or a door station. PoE comes in classes: 802.3af at about 15 W a port, 802.3at at about 30 W and 802.3bt for higher-power kit, all within the switch's total budget.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. An undersized switch is a common cause of cameras that vanish after dark in Greater Manchester properties we are called to. On longer runs we also check cable grade and length, since voltage drop on thin or copper-clad cable can starve a device.

Faceplates, back boxes and the comms cabinet

A data point is a faceplate with one or two RJ45 sockets, fed by its own cable back to a patch panel. Flush back boxes are used where we can chase or drop cable inside a stud wall; elsewhere we use neat surface trunking. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. Equipment then lives in one place with power and airflow, which helps reliability. For shared buildings in Greater Manchester we put the cabinet in a landlord-only cupboard so tenants cannot unplug building systems.

Fault finding in Greater Manchester

Slow or dropping networks usually come down to a short list of causes: a failing cable or termination, a loop between switch ports, a duplicate address, an overloaded PoE switch, or Wi-Fi channel clashes. The method is simple: test the line, then the cabling, then the switch and then the Wi-Fi, recording each result. If it turns out to be the line, we give you the evidence to send to your provider.

Send the address, what is not working or what you want added, and photos of the router, cabinet and problem rooms if you can. Same-day or next-day visits can usually be arranged; the cost is price on application, set out in writing before work starts. At handover you get the test results, a labelled plan of points and access points, and the network names and admin details stored with you, not with us. We tidy as we go: cables are fixed, holes filled and replaced kit removed.

If your cameras lost connection after a Sky hub change in Greater Manchester, we reconnect them and set them up to survive the next one.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

What happens on the day

We connect the recorder to the Sky hub by cable, set a DHCP reservation, rejoin any Wi-Fi cameras, set up cloud or P2P viewing and test it on your phone. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

CCTV and door entry on a Sky or BT hub

Every recorder, camera and video door station we fit works with your Sky or BT hub; the question is how the app reaches it from outside. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. Cloud or P2P connection has the recorder dial out to the maker's service, so no ports are opened and the app survives most router changes.

A DHCP reservation on the router keeps the recorder on a fixed local address. Without a reservation, the address can change after a reboot and remote viewing drops.

Router swaps reset everything: Wi-Fi details, address reservations and any port forwarding. Cameras on Wi-Fi disconnect, port rules are gone and the app reports the system offline, while the recorder still records on site. We reconnect each device, set reservations on the new hub, move remote viewing to cloud or P2P where the recorder supports it, and write the settings down for next time.

Power over Ethernet: sizing the switch

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. The switch has a total power budget in watts, and each port has a limit set by its standard: 802.3af gives up to about 15 W, 802.3at about 30 W and 802.3bt more again.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. Cheap copper-clad aluminium cable and long runs cause voltage drop, so we use solid copper for PoE.

Shared houses and blocks in Greater Manchester

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. The usual set-up is one network for building equipment, one for tenants, and the switch locked away in a landlord space. Clear separation avoids the familiar problem of the building's cameras riding on a tenant's line that is then cancelled.

Mesh, extenders, boosters or wired access points

Plug-in extenders and boosters are cheap, but most repeat the signal on one radio, so devices behind them get far less speed than the router delivers. Mesh systems use several nodes that work as one network with one name, and better ones keep a dedicated radio for the link between nodes. Mesh works best with wired backhaul: each node gets a cable to the router, so its radios serve devices instead of relaying.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. They are managed together, so channels and power are set to stop neighbouring units fighting each other. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Solid brick and block walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors absorb Wi-Fi, which is why the back bedroom or the loft conversion often has no signal. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. An outbuilding or garden office normally needs its own cabled or point-to-point link, not a booster on the windowsill.

Where the hub sits makes a big difference; one left in a meter cupboard or on the floor by the front door covers far less. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. We test each room first, so you only pay for the fix the building actually needs.

Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre in Greater Manchester

For a plain gigabit link to a desk, a smart TV or a door station, Cat5e does the job. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

Between buildings, between floors of larger blocks and on any run longer than copper allows, fibre is the answer. Fibre carries no power, which means the far end needs a media converter or switch with its own supply. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

Each data point is an outlet on the wall, usually single or double, with its own run back to the patch panel. We fit them flush where walls allow, or in surface boxes and trunking where chasing a Greater Manchester wall or a listed finish is not sensible. Typical positions are behind a TV, at a desk, by the router, at each access point and at camera or door-station locations.

All runs end at a patch panel, usually in a small wall cabinet with the switch and router alongside. That keeps the router, switch and any CCTV recorder in one ventilated place rather than on a shelf or the hall floor. In a Greater Manchester HMO or block, the cabinet goes in a locked landlord space, not in a tenant's room.

Fault finding in Greater Manchester

Slow or dropping networks usually come down to a short list of causes: a failing cable or termination, a loop between switch ports, a duplicate address, an overloaded PoE switch, or Wi-Fi channel clashes. We test the line speed at the hub first, then each cable, port and access point in turn, so the fix is aimed at the real problem. Where the problem is the provider's line, you get the readings to show them.

Booking, the visit and what you get

Tell us the address and the problem or plan; photos of the router position and the rooms help us scope it. We offer same-day and next-day slots, and the price is on application after the scope is agreed. You can reach us on 07517 806082 by phone or WhatsApp, or at icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

You are left with a list of what was fitted, the test results, labels that match the plan, and the admin passwords handed to you. Work is left neat, with cable fixed, holes made good and old kit removed if you want it gone.

What happens on the day

We cable the recorder to the BT hub, reserve its address, rejoin Wi-Fi cameras, set up cloud or P2P viewing and test it remotely. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

Works with your Sky or BT hub: what to know

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding opens a port on the router to the recorder, which works but exposes the device and breaks whenever the router or its address changes. We prefer cloud or P2P access: the device connects out, nothing is opened inbound, and it copes with router changes better.

We also set a DHCP reservation on the hub so the recorder or door station always gets the same local address. If that is not done, a restart can hand out a different address and remote viewing quietly stops.

When a provider swaps the hub, which happens on upgrades and moves between Sky and BT, the Wi-Fi name, password, reservations and port rules all change. Wi-Fi cameras and doorbells drop off, forwarded ports vanish and the app shows the recorder offline even though it is still recording locally. We reconnect each device, set reservations on the new hub, move remote viewing to cloud or P2P where the recorder supports it, and write the settings down for next time.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

The budget is worked out from each device's maximum draw, with infrared, heaters and motors included, plus headroom for later additions. A switch that runs out of budget switches ports off, which looks like cameras dropping at night or a door station rebooting. On longer runs we also check cable grade and length, since voltage drop on thin or copper-clad cable can starve a device.

Finding the fault, not guessing

When a network is slow or keeps dropping, the cause is usually physical cabling, a switch loop, an address conflict, PoE overload or Wi-Fi interference. The method is simple: test the line, then the cabling, then the switch and then the Wi-Fi, recording each result. Where the problem is the provider's line, you get the readings to show them.

Which Wi-Fi fix fits a Greater Manchester home or office

A plug-in extender or booster repeats the router's signal, and it usually halves the speed for devices connected through it because it receives and sends on the same radio. A mesh kit puts two or more matched nodes around the building, handing devices between them without a second network name. Mesh works best with wired backhaul: each node gets a cable to the router, so its radios serve devices instead of relaying.

Ceiling access points fed by PoE are what we fit when a Greater Manchester building needs coverage on every floor and room. They are set up as one system, with channel and power planning so they cover rooms without interfering. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

Why the signal dies upstairs or at the back

Thick brick walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors soak up the signal, so rooms two walls away from the router struggle. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. Garden offices, garages and outbuildings in Greater Manchester are usually out of reach of an indoor router altogether.

Router position matters as much as the walls: a hub in a cupboard, behind the TV or by the front door at floor level loses much of its range. In Greater Manchester flats and terraces, dozens of neighbouring networks compete for the same channels. We measure signal and speed room by room, then fix the cause rather than just adding hardware.

Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre in Greater Manchester

Cat5e still carries gigabit Ethernet to a desk, a TV or a camera, and it is the cheapest copper to run where the building only needs 1 Gb/s. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Keeping tenant Wi-Fi apart from building systems

In an HMO or block, tenant broadband and building systems such as CCTV, door entry and fire alarm signalling should not share one open network. The usual set-up is one network for building equipment, one for tenants, and the switch locked away in a landlord space. It also makes it clear who owns which line when a Greater Manchester tenant moves out or a provider contract changes.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

A data point is a faceplate with one or two RJ45 sockets, fed by its own cable back to a patch panel. We fit them flush where walls allow, or in surface boxes and trunking where chasing a Greater Manchester wall or a listed finish is not sensible. Common spots are the TV wall, home-office desks, the router position, ceiling access points and camera points.

At the central point the cables terminate on a patch panel in a cabinet, where short patch leads connect them to the switch. Equipment then lives in one place with power and airflow, which helps reliability. In Greater Manchester blocks and HMOs the cabinet usually sits in a locked landlord cupboard, apart from tenant areas.

We test each room first, so you only pay for the fix the building actually needs.

Choosing the cable grade for Greater Manchester sites

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 is the normal grade we fit in Greater Manchester today because it costs little more than Cat5e and leaves room for faster equipment. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Because fibre carries data only, we plan a powered switch or converter at the remote end. You get the cable grade written on the quote, run by run, with the reason for each choice.

Adding data points and a patch panel in Greater Manchester

A data point is a faceplate with one or two RJ45 sockets, fed by its own cable back to a patch panel. In plastered walls we go flush where we can, and use surface trunking in solid walls, rented flats or finished rooms where chasing is unwelcome. Most jobs put points at the TV, desks, ceiling access points and any camera, recorder or door-entry location.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. It gives the router, switch and recorder a tidy, ventilated home instead of a tangle behind the sofa. In Greater Manchester blocks and HMOs the cabinet usually sits in a locked landlord cupboard, apart from tenant areas.

Finding the fault, not guessing

Slow or dropping networks usually come down to a short list of causes: a failing cable or termination, a loop between switch ports, a duplicate address, an overloaded PoE switch, or Wi-Fi channel clashes. We test the line speed at the hub first, then each cable, port and access point in turn, so the fix is aimed at the real problem. If it turns out to be the line, we give you the evidence to send to your provider.

Does video door entry work with a BT hub?

job/cctv-remote-viewing-setup.html:
Remote viewing for Greater Manchester CCTV systems, set up so it keeps working when the router changes.

We work from 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport SK2 5DE and cover the 60 Greater Manchester towns listed below for this work, with same-day and next-day visits available. Price is on application once the scope is clear.

What happens on the day

We connect the recorder, reserve its address, set up the app with cloud or P2P access, change default passwords and test viewing off-site. We explain the findings before any extra work, and nothing beyond the agreed scope is done without your say-so.

Router swaps, port forwarding and cloud apps

The kit works with your Sky or BT hub; what matters is the remote-access method. Port forwarding points a router port at the recorder; it works, but it puts the device on the internet and fails if the router is replaced. We prefer cloud or P2P access: the device connects out, nothing is opened inbound, and it copes with router changes better.

We also set a DHCP reservation on the hub so the recorder or door station always gets the same local address. Without a reservation, the address can change after a reboot and remote viewing drops.

A new hub from Sky or BT arrives with a new network name, password and blank settings, so Wi-Fi cameras and door stations lose their connection. Wi-Fi cameras and doorbells drop off, forwarded ports vanish and the app shows the recorder offline even though it is still recording locally. On a visit we rejoin each device, redo the reservations, switch to cloud access where possible and leave a written note of the settings.

Landlords and HMOs: tenant broadband and building systems

Tenant Wi-Fi and building systems are better kept apart, so a tenant cannot unplug or reach the CCTV recorder. The usual set-up is one network for building equipment, one for tenants, and the switch locked away in a landlord space. It keeps ownership clear when tenants change or a line is cancelled, which is a common cause of cameras going offline in Greater Manchester HMOs.

Getting the PoE budget right in Greater Manchester

With PoE, a single Ethernet cable powers the device at the far end, which is why it suits cameras and ceiling access points. Each PoE switch has an overall budget and per-port limits; 802.3af ports supply roughly 15 W, 802.3at roughly 30 W and 802.3bt up to 60 W or more.

We add up the worst-case draw of every device, including camera heaters, infrared at night and pan-tilt motors, and leave spare capacity for one or two more. When a budget is exceeded the switch cuts power to some ports, often at night, and cameras appear to go offline for no reason. We only use solid copper cable for PoE; copper-clad aluminium heats up and drops voltage.

Mesh Wi-Fi compared with boosters and extenders

A plug-in extender or booster repeats the router's signal, and it usually halves the speed for devices connected through it because it receives and sends on the same radio. Mesh systems use several nodes that work as one network with one name, and better ones keep a dedicated radio for the link between nodes. Mesh works best with wired backhaul: each node gets a cable to the router, so its radios serve devices instead of relaying.

For offices, HMOs and bigger Greater Manchester homes, ceiling-mounted access points on PoE give the most even coverage. Each unit is tuned for channel and transmit power so coverage overlaps cleanly. Not every job needs cabling: sometimes moving the router and adding one mesh node is the answer.

What causes Wi-Fi dead spots

Thick brick walls, chimney breasts and concrete floors soak up the signal, so rooms two walls away from the router struggle. Foil-backed insulation boards, mirrored wardrobes, underfloor heating and metal stud walls block it further, and kitchens add fridges and microwaves. An outbuilding or garden office normally needs its own cabled or point-to-point link, not a booster on the windowsill.

Router position matters as much as the walls: a hub in a cupboard, behind the TV or by the front door at floor level loses much of its range. Busy channels from neighbours in Greater Manchester terraces and blocks add interference that looks like a weak signal. A walk-round with a meter shows where the signal drops, so the fix targets the real cause.

Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a or fibre in Greater Manchester

Cat5e is rated for gigabit Ethernet, which is plenty for most homes, a single camera or a desk phone. Cat6 adds headroom: it handles gigabit comfortably and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs, so it is our usual choice for new data points in Greater Manchester offices and flats. Cat6a is thicker and stiffer, carries 10 Gb/s to the full channel length and suits Wi-Fi 6 and 6E access points or comms rooms that will be upgraded later.

When a link has to cross a yard, reach an outbuilding or climb several floors, fibre avoids the length limit and electrical issues that copper has between buildings. Fibre carries no power, which means the far end needs a media converter or switch with its own supply. The quote names the grade for each run so you know what is being installed.

Data points, faceplates and patch panels

Each data point is an outlet on the wall, usually single or double, with its own run back to the patch panel. We fit them flush where walls allow, or in surface boxes and trunking where chasing a Greater Manchester wall or a listed finish is not sensible. Typical positions are behind a TV, at a desk, by the router, at each access point and at camera or door-station locations.

The cables meet at a patch panel in a cupboard, under-stairs space or wall cabinet, with a switch beside it. Equipment then lives in one place with power and airflow, which helps reliability. In Greater Manchester blocks and HMOs the cabinet usually sits in a locked landlord cupboard, apart from tenant areas.

Fault finding in Greater Manchester

Slow or dropping networks usually come down to a short list of causes: a failing cable or termination, a loop between switch ports, a duplicate address, an overloaded PoE switch, or Wi-Fi channel clashes. The method is simple: test the line, then the cabling, then the switch and then the Wi-Fi, recording each result. Where the problem is the provider's line, you get the readings to show them.

Booking, the visit and what you get

Start by sending the address, a short description and, if possible, photos of the hub, any cabinet and the rooms affected. Same-day and next-day visits are available, and price is on application once we know the building and the scope. Call or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email icomplypropertyservices@gmail.com.

At handover you get the test results, a labelled plan of points and access points, and the network names and admin details stored with you, not with us. Work is left neat, with cable fixed, holes made good and old kit removed if you want it gone.
